project: Rosnet Case Study — URL Health Monitor
about: Decision log for defending choices in the Rosnet panel. Each decision lists alternatives, tradeoffs, a plain (STE-100) explanation, and how AI was involved. Edge cases are logged here and fixed only at the end, by priority.

timebox.notes: Clock starts with the first line of application code. Planning and setup before that are logged separately below.

decisions.title: C# with ASP.NET Core 10 Minimal APIs
decisions.decision: Build the backend in C# on ASP.NET Core 10 (current LTS) using Minimal APIs.

alternatives.whyNot: My strongest language, but Rosnet is a .NET shop and the brief encourages C#/ASP.NET Core.
More files and ceremony for about five endpoints.

decisions.rationale: Matches Rosnet's stack. Minimal APIs keep each endpoint to a few lines, close to Express route handlers.
decisions.tradeoffs: I am newer to C#, so I must learn and explain backend concepts as I go (tracked in docs/CONCEPTS.md).
decisions.plain: The server is written in C#. Rosnet uses C#. Minimal APIs let us write each web address handler in a few lines, like Express.

decisions.title: React 18 + Vite, no frameworks
decisions.decision: React 18 built with Vite. Plain CSS and native fetch. No Next.js, Tailwind, UI kits, or chart libraries.

alternatives.whyNot: Server rendering and routing are not needed for one dashboard page. Heavier.
Deprecated.
No JSX without a build step; awkward to work with.

decisions.rationale: Vite is a build tool, not a framework. It gives JSX and a fast dev server with very few dependencies.
decisions.tradeoffs: The Vite React template now installs React 19, so React 18 must be pinned on purpose.
decisions.plain: Vite turns our React files into files a browser can read. It does not add rules about how to build the app.

ai.suggestedBy: me (React 18, no frameworks), Claude (Vite, pin React 18)

decisions.title: Plain JavaScript instead of TypeScript
decisions.decision: Write the frontend in plain JavaScript. Optional JSDoc comments on API helpers for editor hints.

alternatives.whyNot: Costs time inside a 3-hour cap. Its main win here is typing a handful of fetch calls.

decisions.rationale: I can write and defend plain JavaScript fastest. The C# backend is already strongly typed; the only untyped edge is a few API calls.
decisions.tradeoffs: No compile-time check that the frontend matches the API shape. Next step: add TypeScript and generate the client from the OpenAPI spec.
decisions.plain: We write the screen code in plain JavaScript. It is faster for me. We can add TypeScript later.

ai.rejected: TypeScript — I overruled it for time and ownership; Claude agreed on review.

decisions.title: SQLite instead of Postgres
decisions.decision: Store URLs, settings, and check results in a single SQLite file.

alternatives.whyNot: Reviewers would need Docker or a local install before running the app.
History must survive a restart.

decisions.rationale: Zero setup for the panel: clone and run. One process writes small rows on a schedule, which fits SQLite well.
decisions.tradeoffs: SQLite allows one writer at a time and is not shared across servers. Production path: Postgres, with time-based partitioning or TimescaleDB for history.
decisions.plain: SQLite keeps all data in one file. Nothing extra is needed to run it. A big real system would use Postgres.

decisions.title: Dapper instead of EF Core
decisions.decision: Use Dapper over Microsoft.Data.Sqlite with hand-written SQL. Create tables with one SQL script at startup.

alternatives.whyNot: Heavier, generates SQL I would need to explain, migrations add setup. Like Prisma: more hidden behavior.
No extra package, but much more boilerplate to map rows to objects.

decisions.rationale: Two small packages. Every query is visible SQL I can read and defend, like using 'pg' or 'better-sqlite3' in Node.
decisions.tradeoffs: No migrations; schema changes are manual. Fine for a take-home, not for a long-lived product.
decisions.plain: Dapper runs SQL that we write. It turns each row into a C# object. We can read every query.

decisions.title: Scheduler: BackgroundService + PeriodicTimer, no job library
decisions.decision: One BackgroundService ticks on a PeriodicTimer, finds URLs that are due (per-URL interval), and checks them in parallel with a concurrency cap and a per-request timeout via IHttpClientFactory.

alternatives.whyNot: Extra dependency and storage tables for a single recurring job.
More moving parts to start, stop, and update when intervals change.

decisions.rationale: Built into .NET. A single 'what is due now?' loop makes per-URL intervals simple and interval changes take effect on the next tick.
decisions.tradeoffs: Runs in one process only; two app instances would double-check. Fine for this scope.
decisions.plain: A loop wakes up every few seconds. It finds the web addresses that need a check now. It checks them at the same time, but not too many at once.

decisions.title: One process serves the API and the built UI
decisions.decision: ASP.NET Core serves the built React app from wwwroot. In development, Vite proxies /api to the backend.

alternatives.whyNot: Reviewers would need to start two things and deal with CORS.

decisions.rationale: One command to run the demo, no CORS setup.
decisions.tradeoffs: Frontend must be built before running the backend in 'production' mode.
decisions.plain: One program sends both the data and the web page. You start one thing.

decisions.title: Configurable intervals: per-URL check interval, history window, retention
decisions.decision: In scope: each URL has its own check interval; the UI picks a history time window; a global retention period deletes old results.

alternatives.whyNot: Simpler, but I want the UI to configure checks per URL.

decisions.rationale: Per-URL intervals fall out of the 'what is due now?' scheduler (D-006) at low cost. Retention is one DELETE query on a timer. History window is a query parameter.
decisions.tradeoffs: Per-URL intervals are listed as bonus scope in the brief and add risk to the 3-hour cap. Claude flagged this; I kept it.
decisions.plain: You can set how often each web address is checked. You can pick how far back to look. Old results are deleted after a set time.

decisions.title: Test core requirements only; log edge cases for the end
decisions.decision: xUnit tests cover only core behavior: a check records status, response time and healthy/unhealthy (including unreachable = unhealthy); results persist; history reads back. Edge cases are logged in edgeCases and fixed at the end by priority if time allows.

alternatives.whyNot: Does not fit 3 hours; the brief warns against shallow tests piled up for a number.

decisions.rationale: The brief asks what was tested, what was skipped, and why. A ranked edge-case list answers that directly.
decisions.tradeoffs: Known gaps exist on purpose and are documented.
decisions.plain: We test the main jobs first. We write down the rare problems. We fix them at the end if there is time.

decisions.title: Light dependencies, visible AI use, decision log in the repo
decisions.decision: Ask before adding any package. Commit log.json and docs/CONCEPTS.md. Keep Co-Authored-By: Claude on AI-assisted commits. Use GSD (open-gsd/gsd-core) for planning.

alternatives.whyNot: The panel explicitly asks how AI was used and what was thrown out; the log is the evidence.

decisions.rationale: Shows the decision process and honest AI use, which the brief says it will dig into.
decisions.tradeoffs: The panel sees my learning notes for backend concepts. That is intentional.
decisions.plain: We keep few add-on packages. We show where AI helped. We save our reasons in the project.

decisions.title: Context management: fresh session per GSD step instead of /compact
decisions.decision: Run each GSD step (discuss, plan, execute, verify) in a new session. State lives on disk in .planning/, log.json and docs/CONCEPTS.md. Use /gsd-pause-work and /gsd-resume-work for mid-phase stops.

alternatives.whyNot: Each summary loses detail; decisions and reasoning drift over time.
Could not be verified in this setup; GSD already provides phase-sized steps with on-disk state.
Runs all phases without stopping; I need to make and understand each decision to defend it.

decisions.rationale: Fresh sessions start with a clean context and read only the files they need. Execution already runs in subagents with their own context.
decisions.tradeoffs: Each new session spends a little time re-reading state files.
decisions.plain: We start a new chat for each step. The plan and notes are saved in files. The new chat reads the files and continues.

decisions.title: Four extras in v1 as a stretch tier, built last
decisions.decision: Pause/resume, check now, URL detail view, and response-time sparkline are v1 but built after all core requirements, in that order, and cut from the bottom if the 3-hour cap is reached. Deferred edge cases (EDGE-01) come after the extras.

alternatives.whyNot: Risks a half-done core if time runs out.
Each is cheap and shows UX judgment; worth attempting once the core is safe.

decisions.rationale: Core value is protected first. Order is cost-to-value: pause/resume and check now are small backend additions; the detail view adds a screen; the sparkline is polish.
decisions.tradeoffs: Total scope is large for 3 hours. Whatever is cut gets listed in the README as next steps.
decisions.plain: We build the main parts first. Then we add the extra parts, one at a time. If time ends, we stop and write down what is left.

edgeCases.title: Overlapping checks for the same URL
edgeCases.description: A slow check (near the timeout) is still running when the URL is due again, so two checks run at once.
edgeCases.plain: A check can take a long time. The next check can start before the first one ends.

edgeCases.title: Very short intervals
edgeCases.description: A 1-second interval would hammer the target and flood the database. Needs a minimum.
edgeCases.plain: If you check too often, you send too much traffic. We need a smallest allowed time.

edgeCases.title: Invalid URL input
edgeCases.description: Missing scheme, non-http(s) scheme, garbage text, or localhost/internal addresses entered in the form.
edgeCases.plain: A person can type a bad web address. The app must say no.

edgeCases.title: Duplicate URLs
edgeCases.description: The same URL added twice, including trailing-slash or case differences.
edgeCases.plain: The same address can be added two times.

edgeCases.title: Time zones in the UI
edgeCases.description: Store UTC; display local time consistently.
edgeCases.plain: The server keeps one world time. The screen must show your local time.

edgeCases.title: TLS certificate errors
edgeCases.description: Expired or self-signed certificates — record as unhealthy with a clear reason vs. a generic failure.
edgeCases.plain: Some sites have a bad security certificate. We should show that reason.

edgeCases.title: Redirect loops
edgeCases.description: Too many redirects; also whether a 3xx counts as healthy.
edgeCases.plain: A site can send you to another address again and again.

edgeCases.title: Deleting a URL that has history
edgeCases.description: Decide whether results are removed with it or kept.
edgeCases.plain: If you remove an address, what happens to its old results?

edgeCases.title: Interval changed while a check is running
edgeCases.description: New interval should apply from the next due time without a restart.
edgeCases.plain: You change the time while a check runs. The new time must start on the next check.

edgeCases.title: SQLite write contention
edgeCases.description: Many parallel checks writing at once could hit 'database is locked'.
edgeCases.plain: Many writes at the same time can block the data file.

edgeCases.title: Huge response bodies
edgeCases.description: Avoid downloading large bodies; only headers are needed for status.
edgeCases.plain: Some pages are very big. We only need the first part of the answer.

aiNotes.note: Claude recommended TypeScript for typed API calls. I rejected it for time and because I can defend plain JS faster. See D-003.
Claude flagged per-URL intervals as bonus scope and a risk to the 3-hour cap. I kept them in scope. See D-008.
Claude flagged that adding all four extras on top of three configurable intervals risks the 3-hour cap. Kept them, but moved them to a stretch tier built after the core. See D-012.
